chapters.title: Chapter 4: Beyond Black-Scholes: Extensions of the Toolkit

lessons.title: Capstone Case Study: Pricing a Real Nifty Option and Reading the Volatility Smile

children.text: Rohan's final assignment as the newest hire on the desk: build a small internal tool that takes a real Nifty options chain, one spot price and five quoted call prices across five strikes, and reports back each strike's implied volatility. It sounds like a formula lookup. It turns out to be the entire course in miniature: pricing theory, a numerical root-finder, and a direct, hands-on encounter with exactly the skew Chapter 4's third lesson described but never showed being extracted from real quotes.

body.text: Pricing a mini options chain end to end, then inverting each quoted price back into its own implied volatility, brings the entire course full circle: the same Black-Scholes formula derived from first principles in Chapter 3 is also the tool that reveals, strike by strike, exactly where and how its own constant-volatility assumption fails against real market prices.

children.text: The Setup: A Mini Nifty Option Chain

body.caption: An illustrative Nifty option chain: spot 24,000, r = 7%, τ = 0.25 years

children.text: Step 1: Price Every Strike With a Single Assumed Volatility

If Black-Scholes's constant-volatility assumption were literally true, one σ, say the at-the-money 24,000 strike's own implied volatility of 11.5%, should price every other strike correctly too. Plug 11.5% into the Chapter 3 formula for the 22,000 strike instead of its actual quote.

stats.label: Price using ATM's 11.5% for every strike
stats.context: Same formula, wrong assumption: one flat σ everywhere

stats.label: Mispricing
stats.context: The single-σ model underprices this strike by this much

body.text: A single flat volatility genuinely misprices the wings of a real options chain, not by a rounding error, but by a real, tradeable ₹37.32 on this strike alone. This is the concrete, rupee-denominated version of Chapter 4's third lesson: the volatility smile is not an academic curiosity, it is the market correcting for exactly this kind of single-σ mispricing.

children.text: Step 2: Back Out Each Strike's Own Implied Volatility

The Black-Scholes formula has no algebraic inverse for σ, so implied volatility is found numerically: guess a σ, price the option, compare to the real quote, and adjust, repeating until the two match. Bisection, halving the search range on each guess, is slower than the Newton-Raphson method traders often use, but is simple and always converges, no derivative required.

body.caption: A bisection-based implied volatility solver, applied to the full chain

body.title: Implied volatility recovered from the mini option chain

children.text: The solver recovered exactly the downward-sloping skew this lesson's quotes were built from, confirming the round trip works: a genuine market pattern, encoded into option prices, extracted back out through nothing but the Black-Scholes formula run in reverse. This is precisely the shape Chapter 4's third lesson attributed to stochastic volatility and its leverage effect, and Chapter 4's fourth lesson connected to jump risk, real markets can gap down hard, so protection against that gap, a deep out-of-the-money put, command a persistently higher price, and therefore a higher implied volatility, than the math of constant-σ GBM alone would ever produce.

body.text: A trader reading this skew does not conclude Black-Scholes is useless, quite the opposite. The formula is precise enough, and standard enough, that any deviation from a flat implied volatility line is immediately visible and quotable. That skew line is the market's own honest correction layered on top of a known, well-understood model, not evidence the model should be discarded. Skew shape and steepness are themselves traded information, often steepening further ahead of known uncertain events like a Budget announcement or an election result.

body.title: Interpret the mispricing
body.question: Why does using the at-the-money strike's 11.5% implied volatility to price the 22,000 strike produce a price (₹2,399.53) below the actual quoted price (₹2,436.85)?
options: Because the Black-Scholes formula itself has an error at strikes far from the money
Because the real 22,000 strike's own implied volatility (14.5%) is higher than the ATM's, and a lower assumed σ understates the option's true value
Because interest rates affect only at-the-money options
Because deep in-the-money options cannot be priced with Black-Scholes at all
body.explanation: The 22,000 strike genuinely trades at a higher implied volatility, 14.5%, than the ATM strike's 11.5%. Feeding in the lower ATM volatility instead systematically understates the option's true price, exactly the ₹37.32 gap computed above. The formula is not wrong; the input volatility was simply the wrong one for that specific strike.

body.title: State the mispricing directly
body.prompt: Using this lesson's numbers, what is the mispricing, in rupees, at the 22,000 strike when a single ATM volatility of 11.5% is used instead of the strike's own 14.5%? (Quoted price ₹2,436.85, single-σ price ₹2,399.53.)
body.explanation: ₹2,436.85 - ₹2,399.53 = ₹37.32. This is not rounding noise; it is the real, rupee-denominated cost of assuming one flat volatility across an entire options chain, on a single contract.

cards.definition: A numerical root-finding method, such as bisection or Newton-Raphson, that inverts the Black-Scholes formula to recover the σ consistent with an observed market price.
The pattern, visible directly in this lesson's recovered implied volatilities, of lower strikes trading at systematically higher implied volatility than higher strikes.

points: This course's full arc: Chapter 1 built the Wiener process from a coin-flip random walk, proved it continuous yet nowhere differentiable, and showed its quadratic variation equals t, the fact ordinary calculus cannot ignore.

Chapter 2 turned that fact into Ito's lemma, derived it rigorously via Taylor expansion, and used it to solve geometric Brownian motion in exact closed form, revealing the lognormal distribution and the -σ²/2 correction.

Chapter 3 built a riskless delta-hedged portfolio, derived the Black-Scholes PDE (discovering μ vanishes entirely), solved it via the Feynman-Kac expectation, and rigorously justified the risk-neutral shortcut with Girsanov's theorem.

Chapter 4 extended the toolkit to puts (proved via a three-line martingale argument), correlated multi-asset baskets (rederiving Markowitz's variance formula), stochastic volatility, jump-diffusion, and finally this capstone, pricing a real chain and recovering its skew.

The mispricing computed in this lesson, ₹37.32 on a single contract from using one flat volatility, is the entire course's central lesson in miniature: Black-Scholes is not wrong, it is a precise, rigorously derived benchmark whose known, explicit limitations, the seven assumptions listed all the way back in Chapter 3, are exactly what a real trading desk watches, quotes, and prices around every day.

From here, the natural next steps are the topics this chapter named but did not fully derive: Fourier-based pricing under stochastic volatility, jump-risk premia, and the multi-factor extensions of the correlated, multivariate Ito calculus this course has now equipped you to read and extend on your own.
